name: Sleeping on your back

card.summary: Sleeping face-up to dodge pillow creases; the wrinkle benefit has not been tested in trials.
card.note: Position is linked to apnea and reflux in sleep research; no wrinkle trials exist.

quick.overview:
Some looksmaxxers sleep on their backs so the face is not pressed into a pillow, aiming to avoid sleep lines.

Sources note habitual sleep position is associated with wrinkles, but no study detail is given and no trial has tested changing position.
quick.mechanism: The idea is that avoiding repeated compression of facial skin overnight reduces creasing over time. This mechanism has not been tested directly.
quick.risks: Sleep literature links supine sleep to worse positional sleep apnea, reflux after meals and more sleep paralysis in some people. Supine sleep is not discussed as a cosmetic risk.

lead: Sleeping on your back (the supine position) is a sleep habit that some looksmaxxers adopt to keep the face from being pressed into a pillow for hours each night. The aim is to avoid so-called sleep lines, the creases on the forehead, cheeks and around the eyes that practitioners attribute to side or stomach sleeping, and so keep the skin looking smoother and more symmetrical over time.[1][2][3]

Dermatology literature does describe sleep wrinkles as a distinct category. A 2016 review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal by Anson, Kane and Lambros separated sleep wrinkles from expression wrinkles and proposed that compression, shear and stress on the face in lateral or prone sleep may create them; the American Society for Aesthetic Plastic Surgery's press release on the paper calls back sleeping ideal for limiting them.[3][6] A 2026 study in Anais Brasileiros de Dermatologia examined frontal wrinkles in older adults and the association of sleep lines with sleep quality.[4] Wikipedia's wrinkle article lists habitual sleeping position among the factors linked to wrinkling, citing an American Academy of Dermatology resource.[2]

Adults sleep in three main positions: lateral, supine and prone, with lateral the most common.[1] Back sleeping is also the position most associated with positional obstructive sleep apnea, so sleep medicine treats it as a trade-off outside of appearance.[1][5]

chain: Face-up sleep keeps the face off the pillow
Less repeated compression and shear on facial skin overnight
Fewer or shallower sleep lines over time
angle.text: Practitioners sleep face-up so the cheeks, forehead and chin are not pressed into bedding, aiming for fewer sleep creases and a more even face. The review literature on sleep wrinkles describes lateral and prone sleep as the positions that load the facial skin.

paras: The practice consists of lying face up for sleep rather than on the side or stomach, so that the face is not compressed against a pillow or mattress. Some adherents combine it with pillow choice or other overnight habits; the details vary by person.

Sleep-position references describe lateral sleeping as most common in adults, followed by supine and then prone, and report that lateral preference rises with age and body mass index.[1] The Aesthetic Society's release says people spend roughly 65 percent of sleep on the side, 30 percent on the back and 5 percent on the stomach, and shift position about 20 times a night, fewer times as they age; the first position is chosen consciously, while later shifts happen unconsciously.[6] Practitioners therefore often describe back sleeping as a habit that is built with pillows or other cues rather than a position that can be held all night by willpower, a point the release itself notes about conscious change.[6]

The 2016 Aesthetic Surgery Journal review titled "Sleep Wrinkles: Facial Aging and Facial Distortion During Sleep" distinguishes sleep wrinkles from expression wrinkles, which differ in cause, location and pattern. It proposes that compression, shear and stress from lateral or prone positions may create wrinkles and may also contribute to expansion of facial skin.[3] According to the Aesthetic Society, lead author Goesel Anson said sleep wrinkles form in response to distortion created when the face is pressed against any sleep surface; the paper appeared online on 20 June 2016, and the society's press release followed on 26 July 2016.[6]

The release adds that sleep wrinkles most often appear on the forehead, lips and cheeks, run mostly perpendicular to expression lines (although some reinforce them), and become more pronounced as skin thins and loses elasticity. It states that botulinum toxin is unlikely to help because the lines are not caused by muscle movement, that dermal fillers can temporarily improve wrinkles of any type, and that non-invasive collagen-stimulating treatments may reduce sleep wrinkles. Its recommendations are to sleep on the back, with specialty pillows as an aid, alongside sun protection, not smoking, nutrition and consistent skincare.[6]

Wikipedia's wrinkle article lists habitual sleeping position alongside glycation, loss of body mass and sun damage as processes linked to wrinkles, and cites the American Academy of Dermatology's aging-skin resource for the statement.[2] It also describes a misrepair-accumulation theory in which repeated stretching and compression of skin injures elastic and collagen fibres, which are replaced by altered fibres, leading to folds.[2]
A 2026 paper in Anais Brasileiros de Dermatologia by Campos and colleagues reports on prevalence and patterns of frontal wrinkles in elderly people and on how sleep lines relate to sleep quality.[4]

sections.h: Other evidence on side sleeping and the face
paras: A Science Focus overview reports that a 2022 ophthalmology-journal study found that people with a preferred sleep side had significantly lower upper eyelids on that side than the other, with no differences in lower-eyelid position, eyebrow placement or eyelid skin redundancy. The same article says that repeatedly lying on one side has not been definitively proven to cause wrinkles on that side.[7]

The overview also quotes dermatological comparisons of the face to a crust with 'fault lines' along which wrinkles form, and says that wrinkles have three main causes: sleep compression, normal ageing and facial expressions. Brazilian dermatology researchers cited there recommend hydration and back sleeping to reduce stretching and compression of skin, and the article describes 'anti-wrinkle' pillows as unproven.[7]

A Science Focus overview reports that a 2022 ophthalmology-journal study found that people with a preferred sleep side had significantly lower upper eyelids on that side than the other, with no differences in lower-eyelid position, eyebrow placement or eyelid skin redundancy. The same article says that repeatedly lying on one side has not been definitively proven to cause wrinkles on that side.[7]

The overview also quotes dermatological comparisons of the face to a crust with 'fault lines' along which wrinkles form, and says that wrinkles have three main causes: sleep compression, normal ageing and facial expressions. Brazilian dermatology researchers cited there recommend hydration and back sleeping to reduce stretching and compression of skin, and the article describes 'anti-wrinkle' pillows as unproven.[7]

Sleep-medicine reviews describe supine position as the most common phenotype of positional obstructive sleep apnea, in which airway collapse is more frequent when lying on the back than on the side.[5] A 2023 review in Sleep Medicine Reviews defines supine-related apnea as respiratory events at twice the frequency supine as non-supine, reports that obstruction arises more commonly supine at the level of the soft palate and epiglottis, and notes that vibrotactile warning devices worn on the neck or chest have emerged over the last decade as treatments to avoid back sleeping.[5] Wikipedia reports that positional apnea accounts for roughly 56 to 75 percent of regular obstructive sleep apnea cases, and that lying supine soon after eating is linked to laryngopharyngeal reflux and supine sleep to sleep paralysis.[1]

Wikipedia's article on obstructive sleep apnea lists sleeping supine as a risk factor and says sleeping on the side or with the upper body raised may help; it also lists a short lower jaw, a narrow upper jaw and a narrow nasal passage among craniofacial risk factors.[8] People with these conditions are generally treated with positional therapy that moves them off the back, which makes the position a consideration beyond appearance.[5]

Other positions have their own associations in the sleep literature summarised by Wikipedia. Lateral sleeping is the most common adult position, and its share rises with age and body mass index. Animal studies reported the highest glymphatic activity in lateral sleep and the lowest in prone sleep, right-side sleeping is associated with more night-time reflux than left-side sleeping, and back sleeping is the position recommended for infants.[1] A Canadian survey cited there found 39 percent preferring the 'log' position and 28 percent side sleeping with legs bent.[1]

Back sleeping appears in skincare and appearance discussions as a habit that needs no product, and the Aesthetic Society release and Science Focus both list it among general anti-wrinkle measures alongside hydration, sun protection and skincare.[6][7] Plastic surgeons quoted in the Aesthetic Society release advise avoiding side and stomach sleeping but acknowledge that sleep position is difficult to change consciously.[6]

The sleep-wrinkle literature is primarily descriptive. The 2016 Anson, Kane and Lambros review proposes mechanisms by which side and stomach sleeping may create wrinkles, and the 2026 Campos study looks at sleep lines in older adults.[3][4] A 2022 study reported lower upper eyelids on the preferred sleep side.[7] No published trial was found that randomises people to back sleeping and measures wrinkle change.
Studies of supine sleep itself are mainly in sleep medicine, covering positional sleep apnea and its treatment.[5]

timeline.event: Benjamin Spock's book warns against infant back sleeping; later studies link prone sleeping with higher SIDS risk and back sleeping becomes the infant recommendation.[1]

Anson, Kane and Lambros publish a review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal separating sleep wrinkles from expression wrinkles (online 20 June); the Aesthetic Society issues a press release on 26 July.[3][6]
A study reports lower upper eyelids on the preferred sleep side.[7]
A Sleep Medicine Reviews article reviews the classification, epidemiology and treatment of supine-related obstructive sleep apnea.[5]
Campos and colleagues publish a study of frontal wrinkles and sleep lines in older adults in Anais Brasileiros de Dermatologia.[4]

lore.intro: Back sleeping is discussed in skincare and appearance communities as an anti-sleep-line habit, usually citing the 2016 plastic surgery review.[3][6]

claims.claim: Sleeping on your side or stomach creates sleep wrinkles
claims.believers: Plastic surgeons and practitioners say compression, tension and shear against the sleep surface distort the face and, repeated nightly, leave lines on the forehead, cheeks and lips.[3][6]
claims.experts: The 2016 review proposes this mechanism; a Science Focus overview reports that one-sided sleeping has not been definitively proven to cause wrinkles on that side, and no trial has randomised people to positions.[3][7]

claims.claim: Back sleeping is the best position to limit sleep lines
claims.believers: The Aesthetic Society release calls back sleeping ideal and says specialty pillows can help.[6]
claims.experts: Dermatology researchers cited by Science Focus also recommend back sleeping for reducing skin stretching and compression, but no study has measured wrinkle change after switching position.[7]

claims.claim: Botulinum toxin cannot fix sleep wrinkles
claims.believers: The release says sleep wrinkles are not driven by muscle movement, so neurotoxins are unlikely to help.[6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes botulinum toxin as acting by immobilising the muscles that cause wrinkles and as FDA-approved for glabellar lines.[2]

claims.believers: The Aesthetic Society release says specialty pillows can help people stay on their backs, the position it favours for limiting sleep wrinkles.[6]
claims.experts: Science Focus describes anti-wrinkle pillows as unproven and potentially uncomfortable.[7]

claims.claim: Sleeping on one side makes that side of the face droop or age faster
claims.believers: Practitioners who sleep supine aim to avoid unequal pressure on one side of the face, in line with the release's description of distortion against the sleep surface.[6]
claims.experts: A 2022 study found lower upper eyelids on the preferred sleep side but no differences in lower eyelids, eyebrows or skin redundancy.[7]

claims.believers: Practitioners choose back sleeping for appearance, and sleep reviews describe positional therapy that moves patients off the back when apnea is supine-related.[5]
claims.experts: Sleep medicine identifies supine position as the most common phenotype of positional sleep apnea and a trigger for reflux and sleep paralysis in some people.[1][5]
